newsitem.title: USA: Intel buys computer graphics supplier for $420 million.
newsitem.headline: Intel buys computer graphics supplier for $420 million.

text.p: Intel Corp., seeking to expand its expertise in designing chips for computer graphics, said Monday it agreed to buy Chips & Technologies Inc. for about $420 million in cash.
The acquisition will help Intel, the world's largest semiconductor company, shore up one of its weaker spots -- chips that provide 3-D graphics and video capabilities for personal computers.
The personal computer industry, led by Intel, has been working to beef up the graphics capabilities of PCs so that they can play full-screen, full-motion video.
Not only would improved graphics make most computing tasks easier, they would let PC makers expand their turf from offices and studies into people's living rooms, analysts said.

"It's a good strategic fit," said Mona Eraiba, semiconductor analyst at New York investment bank Gruntal & Co. "It's very complementary to Intel," which has made improving the visual capabilities of PCs a strategic priority.

Intel will pay $17.50 a share for each of Chips & Technologies' 22 million shares outstanding, or about $385 million in cash. Intel said it anticipated paying another $35 million to cover employee options, for a total purchase price of about $420 million.
Stock in Chips & Technologies, which is based in San Jose, Calif., jumped $3.06 to $17.06 in heavy trading on the Nasdaq market, where it was one of the most actively traded issues.

Chips & Technologies, located five miles away from Intel's headquarters in Santa Clara, specialises in making chips that handle graphics for PCs. Its customers include Apple Computer Inc., International Business Machines Corp. and Digital Equipment Corp.

The company stumbled two years ago because of fierce competition in the field, but has recovered somewhat by concentrating on chips specifically designed for notebook computers. It got hurt again this year by falling chip prices.
The company had been working with Intel to develop the i740 chip, a next-generation 3-D chip that would compete with top-of-the-line offerings from companies such as S3 Inc. and ATI Technologies Inc.

"We think visual computing is an extremely important thrust," said Stephen Nachtsheim, vice president of Intel's mobile and handheld systems group. Nachtsheim said he expected the transaction to be completed within 60 days.
Jim Stafford, Chips & Technologies' president and chief executive officer, will become Intel's vice president of the desktop products groups.
Chips & Technologies will continue to operate as if it were a separate company for now, offering products under its own name, Nachtsheim said.
Intel will gradually absorb Chips & Technologies' operations into its Graphics Components Division.
Intel stock fell 62.5 cents to $88.56, also on Nasdaq.
